items.stem: Which statement describes the electricity supply in a UK home?

options.text: An alternating supply, of about 230 V, with a frequency of 50 Hz
A direct supply, of about 230 V, with a frequency of 50 Hz
An alternating supply, of 50 V, at a frequency of 230 Hz
A direct supply, of a steady 230 V, with no frequency

items.why: Mains electricity is an ac supply; in the United Kingdom it has a frequency of 50 Hz and is about 230 V.

items.stem: What is the difference between a direct and an alternating potential difference?

options.text: A direct pd stays the same size, but an alternating pd changes size
A direct pd is always low, but an alternating pd is always big
A direct pd acts one way only; an alternating pd keeps reversing
A direct pd comes from the mains; an alternating pd from a cell

items.why: A direct potential difference is always in the same direction; an alternating one repeatedly changes direction.

items.stem: A student connects an oscilloscope first to a cell and then to a low-voltage supply at mains frequency. Which description of the two traces is correct?

options.text: Both traces are flat lines, but the mains line sits much higher up
The cell gives a flat line; the mains trace crosses zero
The cell trace crosses the zero line; the mains gives a flat line
The cell is flat; the mains trace rises and falls but never crosses zero

items.why: A cell gives a direct pd, drawn as a flat line; the mains pd reverses, so its trace goes above and below zero.

items.stem: The UK mains supply has a frequency of 50 Hz. What does this tell you?

options.text: The pd completes 50 full cycles every minute
The supply frequency is actually 230 Hz
The pd between live and neutral is about 50 V
The pd goes through 50 cycles each second

items.why: Hertz means cycles per second, so a 50 Hz supply completes 50 complete cycles each second.

items.stem: Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains using three-core cable. What are the three cores?

options.text: Two live wires together with one neutral wire
The live wire, the neutral wire and the earth wire
The live wire, the neutral wire and a fuse wire
The live wire, the earth wire and a switch

items.why: Three-core cable contains a live wire, a neutral wire and an earth wire.

items.stem: The insulation on the wires in a three-core cable is colour coded. Which row gives the colours correctly?

options.text: Live brown, neutral blue, earth is plain green
Live blue, neutral brown, earth plain green
Live blue, neutral brown, earth green and yellow stripes
Live brown, neutral blue, earth green and yellow

items.why: The specified colour code: live wire brown, neutral wire blue, earth wire green and yellow stripes.

items.stem: A wire inside a plug is covered in blue insulation. What is the job of this wire?

options.text: It completes the circuit back to the supply
It carries the alternating pd from the supply
It carries current away only if there is a fault
It holds the case of the appliance at 0 V

items.why: Blue is the neutral wire, and the neutral wire completes the circuit.

items.stem: Why is the insulation covering each wire in a cable colour coded?

options.text: So that each wire can carry a different sized current
Because coloured plastics insulate at a higher voltage
So that each wire can be identified easily
So the colour shows which wire is at the highest pd

items.why: The insulation covering each wire is colour coded for easy identification.

items.stem: What is the job of the live wire in a mains circuit?

options.text: It takes the current back to the supply after the appliance
It carries a current only if a fault develops in the case
It stops the metal case of the appliance becoming live
It carries the alternating potential difference from the supply

items.why: The live wire carries the alternating potential difference from the supply.

items.stem: What is the purpose of the earth wire in an appliance with a metal case?

options.text: It is a safety wire that stops the appliance becoming live
It completes the circuit so that a current can pass round
It carries the used current away to the ground all the time
It supplies the alternating pd to the metal case

items.why: The earth wire is a safety wire, there to stop the appliance becoming live.

items.stem: A kettle is plugged in and working. Which row gives the potential differences correctly?

options.text: Live to earth about 230 V; neutral to earth about 230 V
Live to earth about 115 V; neutral to earth also 115 V
Live to earth about 230 V; neutral to earth about 0 V
Live to earth about 0 V; neutral to earth is 230 V

items.why: The pd between the live wire and earth (0 V) is about 230 V; the neutral wire is at, or close to, 0 V.

items.stem: When does a current pass along the earth wire of an appliance?

options.text: Whenever the appliance is on
Only when there is a fault
All the time it is plugged in
Whenever the current gets large

items.why: The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault.

items.stem: A lamp is switched off at a switch in the mains circuit, but is still plugged in. Why can the live wire still be dangerous?

options.text: Opening the switch only lowers the pd to a smaller, safer value
The neutral wire feeds a current back along the live wire
It is still at about 230 V relative to earth up to the open switch
The earth wire raises the lamp's case to about 230 V

items.why: The supply is still connected, so the live wire on the supply side of the open switch stays at about 230 V.

items.stem: A person changes a bulb without unplugging the lamp. The switch is open. Standing on a concrete floor, they touch the live contact and receive a shock. Why?

options.text: The earth wire pushes a current out of the ground up through them
The contact is still at 230 V, so a current passes through them
Their body completes the circuit between live and neutral
The open switch left a small pd that still shocked them

items.why: An open switch does not remove the pd, so touching the live contact while on the floor makes a live-to-earth path.

items.stem: A frayed cable lets the bare live wire touch a metal water pipe that runs into the ground. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: No current can pass at all, so the wire overheats and melts
The neutral is at 230 V too, so 460 V drives it
The current keeps flowing one way and only changes in size
There is 230 V across the path, so a large current passes

items.why: Live is about 230 V above earth, and the path has little resistance, so a very large current passes.

items.stem: Why is touching the live wire while standing on wet ground so dangerous, even though only one wire is touched?

options.text: A current passes through them to earth
The ground is always carrying current, so it shocks them
Only 115 V, half the supply, acts across them
The pd across them is 460 V, live plus neutral

items.why: The body provides a connection between the live wire and earth, so a current passes through it.

items.stem: Two devices are connected across the same 12 V supply. Device X draws a current of 2.0 A and device Y draws a current of 0.50 A. Which statement about the two devices is correct?

options.text: Device X has the greater power, so it transfers more energy overall.
Device X has the greater power, so it transfers more energy each second.
Device Y has the greater power, because it draws the smaller current.
Device Y has the greater power, as a smaller current is much safer.

items.why: P = V I, and X has the larger current at the same pd, so X transfers energy at the greater rate.

items.stem: A potential difference of 12 V drives a current of 0.25 A through a circuit device. What is the power transfer in the device?

options.text: 9 W

items.why: P = V I = 12 x 0.25 = 3.0 W, with pd in volts and current in amperes giving power in watts.

items.stem: In the equation P = V I, what does each symbol stand for and in which unit is it measured?

options.text: P is power in W, V is pd in V and I is current in A.
P is power in W, V is the pd in A and I is the current in V.
P is power in W, V is pd in ohms and I is current in A.
P is power in J, V is pd in V, and I is current in A.

items.why: These are the quantities and the units the specification gives for P = V I.

items.stem: A current of 0.60 A flows through a resistor of resistance 12 ohms. What is the power transferred in the resistor?
The current through a fixed resistor is doubled. What happens to the power transferred in the resistor?

options.text: The power becomes four times greater, because P = I^2 R squares the current.
The power becomes two times greater, as current and power are proportional.
The power is unchanged, because the resistance itself has not altered.
The power becomes half as large, because the current is being shared.

items.why: Substituting 2I gives (2I)^2 R = 4 I^2 R, so the power is multiplied by four.

items.stem: Which line gives the units the specification uses for power and for potential difference?

options.text: Power is measured in joules, J, and the pd is measured in volts, V.
Power is measured in watts, W, and pd is measured in amperes.
Power is measured in watts, W, and pd is measured in ohms.
Power is measured in watts, W, and pd is measured in volts, V.

items.why: The specification gives power, P, in watts, W, and potential difference, V, in volts, V.

items.stem: Which line gives the units the specification uses for current and for resistance?

options.text: Current is measured in amperes, A, and resistance in volts, V.
Current is measured in amperes, A, and resistance in ohms.
Current is measured in coulombs, C, and resistance in ohms.
Current is measured in amps, A, and resistance in watts.

items.why: The specification gives current, I, in amperes, A, with amp acceptable for ampere, and resistance, R, in ohms.

items.stem: An electric kettle is plugged into the mains and switched on. Which statement best describes why the kettle is built as it is?

options.text: It is designed to create new energy from the mains supply that it uses.
It is designed to store the electrical energy the mains delivers.
It is designed to bring about a particular energy transfer.
It is designed to use up the current flowing in from the mains.

items.why: Everyday electrical appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers, here to the thermal store of the water.

items.stem: A 2000 W kettle is switched on for 2 minutes. A 100 W lamp is switched on for 1 hour. Which transfers more energy?

options.text: The kettle, because it has the higher power rating of the two appliances.
The kettle, because its rating already gives the energy it transfers.
They are equal, because both of them are supplied by the same mains.
The lamp, because energy transferred depends on the time as well as the power.

items.why: E = P t: 100 W for 3600 s is 360 000 J, while 2000 W for 120 s is only 240 000 J.

items.stem: A hairdryer has a power of 1500 W. It is switched on for 4 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?
A food mixer is plugged into a wall socket and switched on. How is energy transferred while it is in use?

options.text: Electrically from the ac mains to the thermal store of the mixer motor.
Electrically from batteries to the kinetic energy of the motor.
Electrically from the ac mains to the kinetic energy of the motor.
From the mains supply to the chemical store of the mixer.

items.why: A mixer is designed to turn a blade, so the useful transfer is to the kinetic energy of an electric motor.

items.stem: A cordless drill and an electric kettle are both in use. Which statement about their supplies is correct?

options.text: The drill is supplied by batteries and the kettle by the ac mains.
The drill is supplied by the ac mains and the kettle by its batteries.
Both are supplied by the ac mains, as both contain a heating device.
Both are supplied by batteries which are recharged after use.

items.why: Portable appliances are supplied by batteries; appliances plugged into sockets use the ac mains.

items.stem: A lamp is connected to a cell and lights up. Which statement about work in this circuit is correct?

options.text: No work is done, because nothing in the circuit can be seen moving.
Work is done, because the lamp uses up the current.
Work is done, because charge is flowing through the lamp.
Work is done only while the lamp is warming up to temperature.

items.why: Work is done when charge flows in a circuit, and that work transfers energy to the lamp.

items.stem: Which equation does the specification give for the energy transferred by electrical work in terms of power?

options.text: energy transferred = power x time, with the time measured in seconds.
energy transferred = power / time, with the time given in seconds.
energy transferred = power x time, with time given in minutes.
energy transferred = power + time, with the time in seconds.

items.why: This is the equation the specification gives for the energy transferred by electrical work, E = P t.

items.stem: A kettle has a power of 2000 W. It is switched on for 90 s. How much energy does it transfer?
items.why: E = P t = 2000 x 90 = 180 000 J, with the power in watts and the time in seconds.

items.stem: A lamp has a power of 60 W. It transfers 5400 J of energy. For how long was it switched on?
items.why: Rearranging E = P t gives t = E / P = 5400 / 60 = 90 s.

items.stem: Which line gives the equation for energy transferred in terms of charge flow, with the correct units?

options.text: E = Q V, where Q is charge flow in amperes and V is the pd in volts.
E = Q V, where Q is charge flow in coulombs and V is pd in volts.
E = Q / V, where Q is charge flow in coulombs and V is the pd.
E = I V, where I is the current in A and V is pd in volts.

items.why: The specification gives energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference, E = Q V.

items.stem: A motor connected to a 12 V supply takes a current of 5.0 A for 60 s. How much energy is transferred?
An electric motor transfers 5400 J of energy when the potential difference across it is 18 V. What charge flowed through it?
items.why: Rearranging E = Q V gives Q = E / V = 5400 / 18 = 300 C.

items.stem: Which units does the specification give for energy transferred and for time in E = P t?

options.text: Energy in joules, J, and time in minutes, min.
Energy in watts, W, and time in seconds, s.
Energy in joules, J, and time in seconds, s.
Energy is in joules, J, and time is in hours, h.

items.why: The specification gives energy transferred, E, in joules, J, and time, t, in seconds, s.

items.stem: Which units does the specification give for charge flow and for potential difference in E = Q V?

options.text: Charge flow in coulombs, C, and pd in volts, V.
Charge flow in amperes, A, and the pd in volts, V.
Charge flow in coulombs, C, and pd in ohms, Ω.
Charge flow in joules, J, and the pd in volts, V.

items.why: The specification gives charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C, and potential difference, V, in volts, V.

items.stem: A circuit device is switched on. Which statement about the power of the device is correct?

options.text: Its power is the pd across it added to the current through it, giving watts.
Its power is the total energy that it transfers, whatever the time taken.
Its power is the pd across it times the current, and the energy given each second.
Its power is the current through it divided by the pd that is across it.

items.why: P = V I gives the power from the circuit quantities, and E = P t shows the same power as the energy transferred per second.

items.stem: Heater X transfers 30 000 J in 60 s. Heater Y transfers 48 000 J in 120 s. Which heater has the greater power?

options.text: Heater Y, because it transfers more energy altogether than heater X does.
Heater Y, because it was switched on for the longer period of time.
They have equal power, since both transfer their energy steadily.
Heater X, because it transfers 500 J each second and Y transfers 400 J.

items.why: P = E / t: X gives 30 000 / 60 = 500 W and Y gives 48 000 / 120 = 400 W.

items.stem: A cook boils the same pan of water on a 2400 W hob and then on a 900 W hob. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The 2400 W hob transfers more total energy, because it has more power.
The 2400 W hob raises the temperature of the water faster than the 900 W hob.
The 900 W hob raises the temperature of the water more quickly than the 2400 W hob.
The 2400 W hob transfers just 2400 J in total before it is switched off.

items.why: A higher power rating means the thermal store of the water is filled at a greater rate.

items.stem: What is the National Grid?

options.text: A system of cables alone that links all of the power stations to consumers.
A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
A system of power stations that generates all of the energy consumers use.
A system of transformers that increases the energy that is sent to consumers.

items.why: This is the specification's description of the National Grid.

items.stem: Electrical power is transferred from a power station to homes. In which order are transformers used along the way?

options.text: Step-down transformers first, then step-up transformers near the consumers.
Step-up transformers at both ends, to keep the pd high all the way.
Step-up transformers first, then step-down transformers near consumers.
No transformers are needed; the cables carry it straight to homes.

items.why: Step-up transformers raise the pd for the transmission cables; step-down transformers lower it to a much lower value for domestic use.

items.stem: Why is the National Grid an efficient way to transfer energy from power stations to consumers?

options.text: A high pd gives a low current, so less energy is wasted heating the cables.
A high pd makes the energy travel along the transmission cables much faster.
A high pd lowers the resistance of the long cables used in the National Grid.
A high pd increases the power that the power station is able to supply.

items.why: For a given power, raising the pd lowers the current, and the power wasted is I^2 R.

items.stem: A transmission cable of resistance 5.0 ohms carries a current of 1000 A. What power is wasted in heating the cable?
items.why: P = I^2 R = 1000^2 x 5.0 = 5 000 000 W wasted in heating the cable.

items.stem: Two insulating materials are rubbed against each other. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other one.
Rubbing creates fresh charge on the surface of each material.
Protons are rubbed off one material and on to the other.
Electrons are rubbed off both materials into the nearby air.

items.why: This is the specification's own account: negatively charged electrons move from one material on to the other, leaving the giver positive and making the receiver negative.

items.stem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. What has happened to the cloth?

options.text: It has gained some protons from the rod, so it is positively charged.
It has lost electrons to the rod, so it is now positively charged.
It has lost all of its charge, so it now has no charge at all.
It has made new positive charge on its surface while rubbing.

items.why: The rod became negative by gaining electrons, and those electrons came from the cloth. Losing electrons leaves the cloth with an equal positive charge.

items.stem: Why is the positive charge left on one rubbed material always equal in size to the negative charge on the other?

options.text: Rubbing always produces equal amounts of the two charges at once.
Both of the materials are rubbed with exactly the same steady force.
Every electron lost by one is an electron gained by the other.
Charge always spreads out evenly between the two materials.

items.why: The two charges are the two sides of one transfer, so counting electrons on either side must give the same number.

items.stem: A student rubs a metal rod held in her bare hand with a dry cloth. The rod shows no sign of being charged. Why not?

options.text: The metal was not rubbed hard or long enough to become charged.
Rubbing a smooth metal surface is unable to create any charge.
The rod gains and loses equal numbers of electrons as it is rubbed.
Charge on the rod flows away through her hand and body.

items.why: A metal conducts, so any charge produced does not stay on the rod: it leaks to earth through the student. Charging by rubbing needs an insulating material.

items.stem: Two charged objects are brought close together but do not touch. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Two objects with the same type of charge attract each other.
Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel each other.
The objects only push or pull when their surfaces touch.
Two objects with different charges repel one another.

items.why: This is the specification statement: like charges repel, and the force acts without the objects touching.

items.stem: Two polythene rods are each rubbed with the same dry cloth. One rod hangs freely on a thread. The second rod is held close to it, without touching. What happens, and why?

options.text: The hanging rod swings away, because rubbing magnetised them.
The hanging rod swings towards it, because charges attract.
The hanging rod swings away, because both carry a like charge.
The hanging rod stays still until the two rods touch each other.

items.why: Rubbing both rods in the same way gives both the same type of charge, and like charges repel across the gap between them.

items.stem: Which observation is the best evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another when they are not in contact?

options.text: A charged rod picks up small pieces of paper when it touches them.
A rubbed plastic rod picks up small iron filings from a nearby dish.
A rubbed rod feels warmer than it did before it was rubbed.
A hanging charged rod turns away as a like charge is put near.

items.why: The rod starts to move while a visible gap remains, so the force must be acting across that gap. It is also repulsion, which rules out an uncharged object being attracted.

items.stem: A charged polythene rod repels a second charged polythene rod. A student says this shows that rubbing has magnetised the rods. Why is the student wrong?

options.text: The force is electrostatic; rubbing only moves electrons.
Magnets repel across a gap, so the two effects must be the same.
Magnetism can only act when two poles are brought into contact.
Two magnetised rods would always attract one another instead.

items.why: Rubbing transfers charge, it does not magnetise. Polythene is not a magnetic material, and the rods behave differently from magnets.

items.stem: A student walks across a nylon carpet and then feels a small shock as her hand nears a metal door handle. What has happened?

options.text: The carpet made new charge, which was stored in the metal handle.
Charge jumps from her hand only once her skin has touched it.
Friction charged her up, and charge then crossed the air as a spark.
The flash is caused by heat from the friction of her shoes.

items.why: Rubbing between shoes and carpet transfers electrons, charging the student. The charge then crosses the gap to the earthed handle as a spark.

items.stem: Charge builds up on an object until a spark suddenly jumps across a gap to a nearby earthed metal pipe. Why does the spark happen?

options.text: Air can never conduct, so the light must come from the metal pipe.
Charge can only cross a gap at the moment two surfaces touch.
The charge on the object grows heavy enough to fall across.
The field grows strong enough for the air in the gap to conduct.

items.why: As charge builds up, the electric field across the gap grows. Once it is strong enough the air stops insulating and charge flows across, which is the spark.

items.stem: Two acetate rods are each rubbed with a dry cloth and both become positively charged. In terms of electrons, why do the rods then repel each other?

options.text: Each rod lost electrons to its cloth, so the like charges repel.
Each rod gained protons from its cloth, so both are now positive.
Rubbing made positive charge on each rod, which pushes them apart.
One rod was rubbed harder, so it holds more charge and pushes away.

items.why: Losing electrons leaves each rod positively charged, and two objects carrying the same type of charge push each other apart.

items.stem: What is an electric field?

options.text: A set of paths that a charged object has to follow.
A region in which a charge experiences a force.
Only the lines drawn around a charge on a diagram.
The charge that has built up on a rubbed object's surface.

items.why: A charged object creates a field around itself, and a second charged object placed anywhere in that region feels a force.

items.stem: How does the strength of the electric field around a charged sphere change as you move further away from the sphere?

options.text: It gets stronger, because the field spreads out as it goes out.
It stays the same up to the last line and then stops there.
It stays exactly the same all around the charged sphere.
It gets weaker; the field is strongest close to the charged sphere.

items.why: The specification states it directly: the field is strongest close to the object and the further away you go, the weaker it is.

items.stem: A charged object is moved closer to a second charged object. What happens to the force between them?

options.text: The force gets stronger as the distance between them decreases.
The force stays the same, as it depends only on the two charges.
The force gets weaker, because the two fields start to cancel.
There is no force at all until the two objects touch.

items.why: The second object sits in a field that is stronger closer in, so the force on it increases as the gap closes.

items.stem: Which description matches the electric field pattern that should be drawn for an isolated charged sphere?

options.text: Circles drawn all the way round the sphere, all evenly spaced out.
Straight lines spreading out from the sphere in all directions.
Straight lines that always point inwards, towards the sphere itself.
Lines that get closer together further out from the sphere.

items.why: The pattern is radial: straight lines evenly spaced all around the sphere, closer together near the surface, with arrows away from a positive sphere.

items.stem: How does the idea of an electric field help to explain the force between two charged objects that are not touching?

options.text: Each object sends out lines that pull the other one along them.
The objects interact only if a field line joins one to the other.
Each object sits in the other's field, so each feels a force.
The air between the objects passes the push from one to the other.

items.why: The field fills the space around each charged object, so neither one has to reach the other: each is already inside a region where it experiences a force.

items.stem: A rubbed polythene rod is negatively charged and the cloth that rubbed it positively charged. They are held close but not touching. What happens?

options.text: They repel each other across the gap.
They attract each other across the gap.
The rod pulls harder, so only the cloth moves across the gap.
No force acts on either until they touch.

items.why: Rubbing left the rod and the cloth with opposite types of charge, and two objects carrying different charges pull together without touching.
